chapters.title: Chapter 3: When Country Risk Turns Into Crisis

lessons.title: Case Study: Sri Lanka's 2022 Default and What Led There

children.text: On 12 April 2022, Sri Lanka announced it would stop paying its external debt, the first sovereign default in the country's history since independence in 1948. What makes Sri Lanka such a useful case study is not that it is exotic or unique. It is that it maps almost perfectly onto the four-stage anatomy from the last lesson, and it does so using nearly every warning sign this course has already introduced: twin deficits, thin import cover, foreign-currency debt concentration, and a currency defended past the point of credibility. This lesson walks through Sri Lanka stage by stage.

markDefs.definition: A bond issued by a sovereign government in a foreign currency, usually US dollars, sold mostly to international commercial investors. Sri Lanka relied heavily on these, unlike India's almost entirely rupee-denominated debt covered in Chapter 1.

children.text: Recall the domestic-versus-foreign-currency comparison from Chapter 1. Sri Lanka sits at the opposite end of that spectrum from India. By the late 2010s, a large share of Sri Lanka's external debt was in commercial

, dollar-denominated debt owed to foreign fund managers rather than concessional loans from multilateral or bilateral lenders. Layered on top of that was Sri Lanka's heavy dependence on tourism and remittances as its main sources of foreign currency, and a long-standing habit of running both a fiscal deficit and a current account deficit, the twin deficits from the last lesson, for years at a stretch. None of this alone was fatal. Together, it built exactly the kind of vulnerability Stage 1 describes: manageable so long as foreign capital kept flowing in, and dangerous the moment it did not.
Most crises in the last lesson's historical table had one clear trigger. Sri Lanka had three, arriving almost back to back, which is a large part of why the outcome was so severe.

First, the April 2019 Easter Sunday bombings badly damaged tourist arrivals, one of the country's largest foreign-currency earners, right as the economy was already slowing. Second, a newly elected government took office in late 2019 and, within weeks, enacted large tax cuts, slashing the VAT rate and corporate taxes, that sharply reduced government revenue at precisely the wrong moment. Third, the Covid-19 pandemic arrived in 2020 and effectively shut down global tourism for close to two years, removing one of Sri Lanka's core sources of foreign exchange almost entirely, while remittance flows also came under pressure.

Then, in April 2021, with forex reserves already under severe strain, the government imposed a sudden, sweeping ban on chemical fertiliser imports, mandating an overnight shift to organic-only farming, explicitly to conserve foreign currency. The policy backfired badly: rice and tea yields, tea being a major export earner, fell sharply, damaging both food security and export revenue at the exact moment the country could least afford either. The ban was reversed within about seven months, but the agricultural damage, and the credibility damage, had already been done.

events.title: Easter Sunday Bombings
events.description: Terrorist attacks devastate tourist arrivals, a major foreign-exchange earner, at a moment the economy was already slowing.

events.title: Large Tax Cuts Enacted
events.description: A newly elected government sharply cuts VAT and corporate tax rates, significantly reducing government revenue just before the pandemic hit.

events.title: Covid-19 Crushes Tourism
events.description: Global travel restrictions remove one of Sri Lanka's largest sources of foreign currency for nearly two years.

events.title: Fertiliser Import Ban
events.description: A sudden mandate for organic-only farming, aimed at conserving forex, sharply cuts rice and tea yields before being reversed roughly seven months later.

events.title: Reserves Collapse
events.description: Usable forex reserves fall to critically low levels, far short of near-term external debt obligations and import needs.

events.title: The Rupee Is Floated
events.description: After defending the currency for months, the central bank lets the rupee float, and it depreciates sharply almost immediately.

events.title: Sri Lanka Defaults
events.description: The government announces a pre-emptive suspension of external debt payments, its first sovereign default since independence in 1948.

events.title: President Resigns Amid Protests
events.description: Widespread shortages of fuel, cooking gas, and medicine trigger mass protests (the 'Aragalaya' movement); the president flees the country and resigns.

events.title: IMF Programme Approved
events.description: The IMF approves an Extended Fund Facility of roughly $3 billion, conditional on tax hikes, subsidy reforms, and a formal debt restructuring.

events.title: Bondholder Restructuring Concludes
events.description: Sri Lanka reaches agreement with international bondholders on restructured terms, including new bonds with payouts partly linked to future economic performance.

children.text: As these shocks compounded through 2020 and 2021, rating agencies cut Sri Lanka's rating repeatedly, moving it from single-B territory deep into CCC and eventually CC ratings, effectively signalling default was imminent, well before the actual event, but importantly, still trailing the market's own repricing, exactly the lag described in the last chapter. Bond yields and CDS spreads widened sharply over the same period as investors priced in rising default risk. Meanwhile, the central bank was spending down its reserves defending the rupee's value rather than letting it adjust, a strategy that works only as long as reserves hold out.

stats.label: Forex Reserves, 2019
stats.context: Already thin relative to Sri Lanka's external obligations

stats.label: Forex Reserves, Early 2022
stats.context: Far short of near-term external debt and import needs, breaching the Greenspan-Guidotti and import-cover thresholds from the last lesson

body.text: This is the last lesson's Greenspan-Guidotti rule and import-cover threshold, both breached, playing out in real life rather than in a hypothetical. Reserves fell far short of covering short-term external obligations, and import cover dropped well below the 3-month danger zone, precisely the combination flagged as the classic pre-crisis setup.

children.text: Stage 4: Default, Collapse, and the Long Road Back

By April 2022, Sri Lanka had run out of road. The government announced a pre-emptive default, suspending payments on the bulk of its external debt rather than draining its last reserves trying to keep paying. The consequences on the ground were severe and immediate: months-long queues for fuel and cooking gas, medicine shortages, and rolling power cuts. Public anger boiled over into the Aragalaya ('struggle') protest movement, and in July 2022 the president fled the country and resigned after protesters occupied the presidential residence, an extraordinary illustration of how directly a sovereign debt crisis can become a political crisis, exactly the feedback loop between the economic and political pillars flagged back in Chapter 2.

Recovery took years, not months. The IMF approved a roughly $3 billion Extended Fund Facility programme in March 2023, conditional on Sri Lanka raising its VAT rate, cutting subsidies, and committing to a credible fiscal consolidation and debt restructuring path, the kind of IMF conditionality this course covers in full in an upcoming lesson. India played a notable regional role too, extending several billion dollars in credit lines and currency swap support through 2022 to help Sri Lanka manage fuel, food, and medicine imports during the worst of the shortage. Formal restructuring talks with bondholders and official creditors, including China, India, Japan, and the Paris Club, stretched on for more than two years before a bondholder agreement was finalised in late 2024, restructuring roughly $12-13 billion of international bonds into new instruments, including some whose payouts are linked to Sri Lanka's future economic performance.

body.title: Sri Lanka vs India: Why the Same Global Shocks Hit So Differently

columns.label: Sri Lanka (Pre-Default)
points: Large share of external debt in commercial dollar bonds (ISBs)
Heavily dependent on a narrow set of forex sources: tourism and remittances
Defended a currency peg-like regime until reserves were nearly exhausted
Compounding domestic policy missteps (tax cuts, fertiliser ban) on top of external shocks

columns.label: India
points: Debt is overwhelmingly domestic and rupee-denominated, as covered in Chapter 1
A diversified external position: goods exports, large services (IT) exports, and broad remittance inflows
A managed float that allows gradual currency adjustment rather than a hard defense to the point of collapse
Substantial forex reserves, well above common adequacy thresholds, as covered in Chapter 2

body.title: Classify the Event
body.scenario: Consider three specific facts from Sri Lanka's crisis: (1) the December 2019 tax cuts, (2) the widening of Sri Lanka's CDS spreads through 2020-21, and (3) the April 2022 suspension of external debt payments.
body.prompt: Map each of these three facts onto the correct stage of the four-stage anatomy from the previous lesson.
body.modelAnswer: The December 2019 tax cuts are a Stage 2 trigger, a domestic policy decision that sharply weakened government revenue just before further shocks hit. The widening of CDS spreads through 2020-21 is a Stage 3 signal, the market repricing default risk in real time, well ahead of the eventual event. The April 2022 suspension of external debt payments is the Stage 4 crisis point itself, the moment vulnerability, triggers, and lost confidence culminated in an actual default.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why did Sri Lanka's fertiliser import ban make its crisis worse, rather than better, despite being explicitly intended to conserve foreign exchange?
options: It had no real effect on the economy either way
It sharply cut yields of rice and export crops like tea, damaging both food security and export earnings, the opposite of the forex relief it was meant to provide
It only affected imports of fertiliser and had no impact on agriculture
It was reversed before it could have any effect on the economy
body.explanation: The policy aimed to save foreign currency by cutting fertiliser imports, but the abrupt, poorly sequenced shift to organic-only farming sharply reduced yields, including tea, a major export earner. That worsened the very foreign-currency shortage the policy was meant to address, while also creating a domestic food security problem, illustrating how a well-intentioned but poorly designed domestic policy can function as a genuine crisis trigger in its own right.

body.text: Sri Lanka did not fall into crisis because of one bad decision or one unlucky shock. It fell because years of foreign-currency-heavy borrowing met three separate shocks in close succession, each one closing off an escape route the last one might have left open. The four-stage anatomy is not a story about villains. It is a story about how vulnerabilities compound.

children.text: This lesson focused on how Sri Lanka's crisis unfolded. The next lesson zooms into one specific mechanism that hit ordinary Sri Lankans directly: how a currency crisis and capital flight translate into everyday hardship for a country's own citizens, not just its bondholders.

points: Sri Lanka's crisis followed the four-stage anatomy closely: years of foreign-currency debt buildup and twin deficits (Stage 1), three compounding triggers, the Easter bombings, 2019 tax cuts, and the pandemic, followed by a self-inflicted fertiliser ban (Stage 2), a rating and market-driven loss of confidence (Stage 3), and a formal default in April 2022 (Stage 4).

Sri Lanka's heavy reliance on commercial dollar bonds (ISBs), unlike India's domestic rupee-denominated debt, meant currency and rollover risk were concentrated exactly where the country was most exposed.
Reserves fell from roughly $7.5 billion in 2019 to under $2 billion by early 2022, breaching both the import-cover and Greenspan-Guidotti thresholds from the previous lesson.
The default triggered severe shortages and, ultimately, the president's resignation in July 2022, a direct illustration of how economic and political risk feed into each other.

Recovery required an IMF programme (approved March 2023) and a multi-year bondholder restructuring that concluded in late 2024, underscoring how long the road back from a sovereign default typically is.

body.text: The reserve levels, debt amounts, and specific dates in this lesson are drawn from widely reported sources on Sri Lanka's 2022 crisis and are presented as approximate where exact figures vary by source. For precise figures, consult the IMF's Sri Lanka country reports, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, or official restructuring documentation.
